## Talk title

**Setting the legal limit with an R package: 15 years from lone scripter to open-source
regulatory infrastructure — and what changed when the AI arrived**

Shorter alternatives:

- *From SourceForge to statute: how open-source R ended up setting water quality limits in
  three countries*
- *White, grey and black: open code, confidential data, and the numbers that stop an operation*
- *Seven years without a test, then four days: an accidental software developer's field notes*

---

## Abstract (250 words) — primary version

When a dredge works off the Pilbara coast, it runs against a number. Cross it and the vessel
stops. Set it wrong the other way and you quietly lose a reef. Somebody has to defend that
number to a regulator, and eventually to a lawyer.

That number came out of R code that I wrote.

I am a quantitative ecologist with sound applied statistics and no training in programming.
This talk is the honest version of how I got from there to maintaining software that sets
water quality limits in three countries.

Three eras. The lone scripter: a 57-script expert-elicitation tool, published in 2012,
distributed as a zip file, unreproducible within five years. Then packages, GitHub, and
industry data I am not allowed to show you — `FSSgam`, `epower`, `bayesnec`, `ssdtools` —
where open code turned out to be the *precondition* for agreement, not a nice-to-have. You
cannot get three regulators to sign off on a black box.

Then the part I did not expect. I stopped writing code by hand in June, and I think I am five
times more productive. That is precisely the claim this audience should distrust, so I
measured it.
Across 1,340 of my own commits: tests tripled as a share of the work, packaging and CI rose
fivefold, and source code went *down*. One package sat seven years without a single test,
then got a suite in four days — which immediately surfaced two bugs it had shipped since
2018.

The judgement, though, is still mine. It has to be.

*(255 words)*

---

## Abstract (150 words) — short version

When a dredge works off the Pilbara coast, it runs against a number. Cross it and the vessel
stops. That number came out of R code that I wrote.

I am a quantitative ecologist with no training in programming who now maintains software
that sets water quality limits in three countries. This talk is the honest version of how
that happened: a 2012 tool that was a 57-script zip file and unreproducible within five
years; then `FSSgam`, `epower`, `bayesnec` and `ssdtools`, and the discovery that you cannot
get three regulators to sign off on a black box.

Then the part I did not expect. I stopped writing code by hand in June and I think I am five
times more productive — so I measured it, across 1,340 of my own commits. The speed-up is not
in the typing, and I will show you exactly where it is.

*(147 words)*

## Speaker biography

Rebecca Fisher is a quantitative ecologist at the Australian Institute of Marine Science,
with over 25 years of experience in marine ecology and more than 100 peer-reviewed papers
and technical reports. Her interests lie at the interface between ecology, numerical
modelling and quantitative decision science, and she is committed to environmental science
research that is of direct relevance to government and industry end users.

Her recent work focuses on statistical ecotoxicology, developing robust tools for
quantifying and handling uncertainty in environmental risk management. She is an author or
contributor to the R packages `ssdtools`, `bayesnec`, `epower`, `FSSgam` and `ElicitN`, and
co-led the joint Australian–Canadian investigation that resulted in `ssdtools` being adopted
as the default software for deriving water quality guideline values.

GitHub: [beckyfisher](https://github.com/beckyfisher) ·
[open-AIMS](https://github.com/open-AIMS)

*(140 words)*
